parts.problem_md:
Fig. 3.1 shows a reaction pathway involving various copper(II) species.

![Flow diagram of reactions converting solid CuSO₄ through intermediates A–D to CuO, Cu(s) and [CuCl₄]³⁻, using H₂O, NH₃, Na₂CO₃, heat and conc. HCl](assets/001-flow-diagram-of-reactions-converting-solid-cuso-.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Construct the equation for the formation of complex **D** from complex **A**.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the formation of complex D from complex A:
> 
> - [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4Cl<sup>–</sup> → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Complex A is the hexaaquacopper(II) ion [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, formed when copper(II) sulfate dissolves in water. Complex D is [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup>, formed when concentrated hydrochloric acid provides excess Cl<sup>–</sup> ions for ligand substitution. The coordination number changes from 6 (octahedral) to 4 (tetrahedral).

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 3.1 shows a reaction pathway involving various copper(II) species.

![Flow diagram of reactions converting solid CuSO₄ through intermediates A–D to CuO, Cu(s) and [CuCl₄]³⁻, using H₂O, NH₃, Na₂CO₃, heat and conc. HCl](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/06/6-2-3a-h-copper-carbonate-reaction-scheme.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Explain why it is not possible to identify complex **B**.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> It is not possible to identify complex B because:
> 
> - The amount of ammonia is not given
> **OR**
> It is not clear if the ammonia is in excess **[1 mark]**
> - A small amount of ammonia forms Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub>
> **AND**
> Excess ammonia forms [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Excess ammonia does not result in full ligand substitution for copper(II): only four of the six water ligands are replaced by ammonia, giving [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, not [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 3.1 shows a reaction pathway involving various copper(II) species.

![Flow diagram of reactions converting solid CuSO₄ through intermediates A–D to CuO, Cu(s) and [CuCl₄]³⁻, using H₂O, NH₃, Na₂CO₃, heat and conc. HCl](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/06/6-2-3a-h-copper-carbonate-reaction-scheme.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

i) Using the information in Fig. 3.1, construct the equation including state symbols to form compound **C** and other products.

[2]

ii) State the type of reaction that occurs when compound **C** is converted into copper(II) oxide.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The equation, including state symbols, to form compound C:

CuSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (aq) → CuCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants and products
> 
> 1 mark for all state symbols correct

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The type of reaction when compound C is converted into copper(II) oxide:
> 
> - Thermal decomposition / thermolysis **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Decomposition' alone is not accepted; 'thermal' must be specified

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i: all species are soluble except copper(II) carbonate (all Group 1 salts are soluble), so CuCO<sub>3</sub> is the precipitate. Compound C is CuCO<sub>3</sub> (s).
> 
> For part ii: copper(II) carbonate breaks down on heating to form copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide. This is thermal decomposition. If you write 'decomposition' alone, you must include 'thermal' to gain the mark.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 3.1 shows a reaction pathway involving various copper(II) species.

Complex A is the hexaaquacopper(II) ion [Cu(H2O)6]2+, formed when copper(II) sulfate dissolves in water. Complex D is [CuCl4]2-, formed when concentrated hydrochloric acid provides excess Cl- ions for ligand substitution.

The oxidation number of copper in [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>3–</sup> is +1.

i) State the electronic configuration of a Cu<sup>+</sup> ion.

[1]

ii) Deduce the role of copper metal in the formation of [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>3–</sup> from the complex **D**.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The electronic configuration of a Cu<sup>+</sup> ion:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The role of copper metal in the formation of [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>3–</sup> from complex D:
> 
> - A reducing agent **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The ground state electron configuration of Cu is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> (copper is an exception to aufbau filling: the 4s<sup>1</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> arrangement is more stable than 4s<sup>2</sup> 3d<sup>9</sup>). When Cu forms Cu<sup>+</sup>, the 4s<sup>1</sup> electron is removed, leaving the stable [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup> configuration.
> 
> In the reaction [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + Cu → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>3–</sup> + Cu<sup>+</sup>, copper metal loses an electron and is oxidised. Because it causes reduction of the complex, it acts as a reducing agent. Remember: reducing agents are themselves oxidised.

parts.problem_md:
Cobalt(II) and copper(II) undergo similar reactions to each other.

Cobalt(II) nitrate and copper(II) nitrate both decompose in a similar manner to that of Group 2 nitrates.

Construct an equation for the thermal decomposition of Co(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the thermal decomposition of Co(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is:
> 
> - Co(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → CoO + 2NO<sub>2</sub> + ½O<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> 2Co(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → 2CoO + 4NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Group 2 metal nitrates thermally decompose to form the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide, and oxygen:
> 
> M(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → MO + 2NO<sub>2</sub> + ½O<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> Cobalt(II) nitrate follows the same pattern. Make sure you give the cobalt(II) nitrate equation, not the copper(II) equation.

parts.problem_md:
Using complex ions formed by Cu<sup>2+</sup> with ligands selected from H<sub>2</sub>O, NH<sub>3</sub>, Cl<sup>–</sup>, C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>, construct an equation for each of the following.

i) A ligand substitution reaction with no change in the coordination number or the charge on the complex ion.

[2]

ii) A ligand substitution reaction with both a change in the coordination number and the charge on the complex ion.

[2]

iii) A ligand substitution reaction with no change in the coordination number but a change in the charge on the complex ion.

[2]

iv) A ligand substitution reaction with the greatest increase in entropy.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
Equations for each type of ligand substitution by Cu<sup>2+</sup> (ligands available: H<sub>2</sub>O, NH<sub>3</sub>, Cl<sup>–</sup>, C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>):

i) No change in coordination number or charge:

[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4NH<sub>3</sub> → [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

**OR**

[Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O → [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4NH<sub>3</sub>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct chemical species
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing

ii) Change in both coordination number and charge:

[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4Cl<sup>–</sup> → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

**OR**

[Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4Cl<sup>–</sup> → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4NH<sub>3</sub>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct chemical species
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing
> 
> Only octahedral → tetrahedral reactions via Cl<sup>–</sup> substitution are accepted
> 
> Reverse reactions are not accepted (entropically unfavourable).

iii) Change in charge but no change in coordination number:

[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 3C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> → [Cu(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>4–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

**OR**

[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + Cl<sup>–</sup> → [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>Cl]<sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct chemical species
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing
> 
> Full Cl<sup>–</sup> substitution is not accepted

iv) Greatest increase in entropy:

[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4–</sup> → [Cu(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

**OR**

[Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4–</sup> → [Cu(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4NH<sub>3</sub>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct chemical species
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read each sub-part carefully and identify exactly what must change and what must stay the same before writing your equation.
> 
> For part iv, entropy increases most when the fewest ligand molecules replace the greatest number of ligands.
> 
> One EDTA<sup>4–</sup> (hexadentate) replaces six monodentate ligands, releasing six water molecules and greatly increasing the number of moles of products.

parts.problem_md:
A solution is made by dissolving CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O in an excess of aqueous ammonia. This solution contains the copper complex [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

i) State the expression for the *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

[1]

ii) State the colour of the solution of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The expression for the *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> = `fraction numerator left square bracket Cu left parenthesis NH subscript 3 right parenthesis subscript 4 right square bracket to the power of 2 plus end exponent over denominator left square bracket Cu left parenthesis straight H subscript 2 straight O right parenthesis subscript 6 right square bracket to the power of 2 plus end exponent left square bracket NH subscript 3 right square bracket to the power of 4 end fraction` **[1 mark]**
> 
> Water / H<sub>2</sub>O must not be included in the *K*<sub>stab</sub> expression.
> 
> ii) The colour of the solution of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - Deep / dark / royal blue **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Kstab expression is constructed like a Kc expression: the concentration of the complex in the numerator, and the concentrations of the separated metal ion and ligands in the denominator. Water ligands are not included (they are the solvent).
> 
> CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O dissolves in water to give [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (pale blue). Adding excess ammonia displaces the water ligands to give [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, which is a characteristic deep/dark blue.

parts.problem_md:
The solution of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is heated gently so that NH<sub>3</sub> is released. A precipitate of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> forms and is collected.

A sample of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> is added to concentrated hydrochloric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Y**.

A sample of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> is added to dilute sulfuric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Z**.

Construct an equation for the reaction of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> to form Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> when the solution is heated.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the reaction of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> to form Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> on heating is:
> 
> - [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + 2NH<sub>3</sub>
> **OR**
> [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> + 4NH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> On heating, the NH<sub>3</sub> ligands are driven off and the remaining water hydrolyses the copper ion to give Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub>. When NH<sub>3</sub> leaves as a gas, some may remain in solution as NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (giving the first equation) or all may leave as NH<sub>3</sub> gas (giving the second equation). Both are acceptable.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A sample of Cu(OH)~2~ is added to concentrated hydrochloric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Y**.

Construct an equation for the reaction of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> with concentrated hydrochloric acid, forming **Y**.
parts.solution_md:
The equation for the reaction of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> with concentrated hydrochloric acid to form **Y** is:

Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 4HCl → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2H<sup>+</sup>

**OR**

Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 4Cl<sup>–</sup> + 2H<sup>+</sup> → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> complex including charge
> 
> 1 mark for the rest of the equation fully correct and balanced

> **[exam-tip]**
> Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> contains Cu<sup>2+</sup> with two OH<sup>–</sup> ions. In concentrated HCl, four Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands (which are larger than water) displace all ligands to give tetrahedral [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup>. The two OH<sup>–</sup> ions react with two of the H<sup>+</sup> ions from HCl to give 2H<sub>2</sub>O, leaving 2H<sup>+</sup> unreacted on the right-hand side.

**[2 marks]**

>

>

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A sample of Cu(OH)~2~ is added to concentrated hydrochloric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Y**.

A sample of Cu(OH)~2~ is added to dilute sulfuric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Z**.

|   | **Y** | **Z** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| colour of complex |   |   |
| geometry of complex |   |   |
| formula of complex | [CuCl~4~]^2-^ |   |

Explain why complexes **Y** and **Z** are coloured and why their colours are different.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Complexes **Y** and **Z** are coloured and have different colours because:
> 
> - The d orbitals split into two sets of energy levels of different energy **[1 mark]**
> - Electrons absorb a specific frequency / wavelength of light / photons **[1 mark]**
> - The absorbed energy promotes / excites electron(s) to the higher energy level **[1 mark]**
> - The colour observed is complementary to the wavelength / colour absorbed **[1 mark]**
> - The d–d energy gap / Δ*E* is different for **Y** and **Z**, so a different frequency / wavelength of light is absorbed for each complex **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The origin of colour in transition metal complexes is frequently identified by examiners as an area students find difficult. The key chain of reasoning is: d orbital splitting causes a specific energy gap; an electron absorbs a photon of that exact energy and is promoted; the colour you see is the complementary colour (what is not absorbed).
> 
> The reason Y and Z have different colours is that they have different ligands (Cl<sup>–</sup> vs H<sub>2</sub>O), which cause different amounts of d orbital splitting, and therefore different frequencies of light are absorbed.

parts.problem_md:
This question is about the transition metal copper.

i) State the full electronic configuration of a Cu atom and a Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion.

[2]

ii) State **four** characteristic features of the chemistry of copper and its compounds.

[4]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The full electronic configurations are:
> 
> - Cu atom: 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion: 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>9</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> For the Cu atom, allow 3d and 4s in either order.
> 
> ii) Four characteristic features of copper and its compounds:
> 
> Any **four** from (1 mark each):
> 
> - Variable oxidation states
> - Forms coloured ions / compounds
> - Forms complex ions
> - Acts as a catalyst
> - Has an incomplete d subshell (in at least one of its common oxidation states)
> 
> **[4 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Copper has the unusual electronic configuration [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> (not [Ar]3d<sup>9</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>), because a fully filled d subshell is particularly stable. When it forms Cu<sup>2+</sup>, it loses the 4s electron and one 3d electron to give a 3d<sup>9</sup> configuration.
> 
> The characteristic features listed above apply to all transition metals. You can remember them as: variable oxidation states, colour, complex formation, and catalytic behaviour.

parts.problem_md:
The chloride ion is a monodentate ligand. When concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> ions the water ligands are replaced.

i) Explain what is meant by the term monodentate ligand.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation to represent the ligand substitution reaction.

[1]

iii) Draw a diagram to show the structure of the complex ion formed.

[1]

iv) State the geometry of the complex ion formed.

[1]

v) State the change in coordination number.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A monodentate ligand is:
> 
> - A ligand that forms one coordinate bond / donates one lone pair of electrons to a central metal atom or ion **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the ligand substitution reaction is:
> 
> - [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4Cl<sup>–</sup> → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

iii) The structure of the complex ion formed is:

![Hand-drawn tetrahedral complex showing a central Cu atom bonded to four Cl ligands with wedge and dashed bonds, in square brackets with a 2− charge](assets/006-hand-drawn-tetrahedral-complex-showing-a-central.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct tetrahedral structure of [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup>
> 
> iv) The geometry of the complex ion formed is:
> 
> - Tetrahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> v) The change in coordination number is:
> 
> - 6 to 4 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A monodentate ligand donates one lone pair of electrons (forms one coordinate bond). The Cl<sup>–</sup> ion has lone pairs available for donation.
> 
> In the ligand substitution, six water ligands (smaller) are replaced by four chloride ions (larger). Fewer ligands can fit around the copper ion when they are larger, so the coordination number drops from 6 to 4 and the geometry changes from octahedral to tetrahedral.

parts.problem_md:
[Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> is an example of a complex ion containing cobalt.

i) Deduce the oxidation state of cobalt in this complex ion. Explain your answer.

[2]

ii) State the geometry of this complex ion.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The oxidation state of cobalt in [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> is:
> 
> - +3 **[1 mark]**
> - The 4 NH<sub>3</sub> ligands are neutral and the 2 Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands each contribute –1 (total –2). The overall charge is +1, so: x + 0 + (–2) = +1, giving x = +3 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The geometry of this complex ion is:
> 
> - Octahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> The complex has six monodentate ligands (4 NH<sub>3</sub> + 2 Cl<sup>–</sup>) around the central Co<sup>3+</sup> ion, which gives an octahedral geometry.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To deduce the oxidation state: set the unknown as x, substitute the charges of all other species (NH<sub>3</sub> = 0, Cl<sup>–</sup> = –1, overall charge = +1), and solve for x.
> 
> The overall charge on the complex tells you about the central metal ion. Here: x + 4(0) + 2(–1) = +1, so x = +3.

parts.problem_md:

An aqueous solution of copper(II) contains the [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> complex ion.

Define the term complex ion.

> A complex ion is:

> **[exam-tip]**
> A complete definition of a complex ion requires two components: the central metal atom or ion, and the ligands surrounding it. A one-sentence answer that includes both components will gain full marks.

parts.problem_md:
Compound **A**, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub>, is a tridentate ligand.

![Structural formula of compound A: a central secondary amine linked to two ethylamine groups, representing diethylenetriamine.](assets/009-structural-formula-of-compound-a-a-central-secon.png)

i) Explain why one molecule of **A** can form three coordinate bonds.

[1]

ii) C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub> reacts with aqueous chromium(III) ions, [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>, in a 2:1 ratio to form a new complex ion.

Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One molecule of **A** can form three coordinate bonds because:
> 
> - Each nitrogen atom has a lone pair of electrons that can be donated to the central metal ion **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for this reaction is:
>

parts.problem_md:
The feasibility of redox reactions can be determined using standard electrode potential, *E*<sup>θ</sup>, values.

The following electrochemical cell is set up.

Pb<sup>4+</sup> (aq) + 2Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → 2Mn<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + Pb<sup>2+</sup> (aq)

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Mn | –1.18 |
| Mn<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Mn<sup>2+</sup> | +1.49 |
| Pb<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Pb | –0.13 |
| Pb<sup>4+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Pb<sup>2+</sup> | +1.69 |

Construct the reduction half-equation and the oxidation half-equation for the reaction.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The half-equations for the reaction are:
> 
> - Reduction: Pb<sup>4+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Pb<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidation: Mn<sup>2+</sup> → Mn<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow ⇌ instead of → in the reduction half-equation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The overall reaction shows Pb going from +4 to +2 (gaining electrons / reduction) and Mn going from +2 to +3 (losing electrons / oxidation). Select the matching half-equations from the table.
> 
> For the oxidation half-equation, reverse the direction from the table: Mn<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Mn<sup>2+</sup> in the table becomes Mn<sup>2+</sup> → Mn<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> when written as an oxidation.

parts.problem_md:
Potassium manganate(VII) can be used to titrate a sample containing an unknown percentage of iron(II).

i) Complete the half-equation for the reduction of manganate(VII) ions, MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>, to manganese(II) ions, Mn<sup>2+</sup>.

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + ........H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + ........e<sup>–</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + ........H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

[1]

ii) State, in terms of electron transfer, whether this half-equation represents oxidation or reduction.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The completed half-equation is:
> 
> - MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 5e<sup>–</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The half-equation represents:
> 
> - Reduction; electrons are gained **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To balance the manganate(VII) half-equation, work in steps.
> 
> - First, balance the oxygens using H<sub>2</sub>O: four oxygens in MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> give 4H<sub>2</sub>O.
> - Then balance the hydrogens using H<sup>+</sup>: four H<sub>2</sub>O require 8H<sup>+</sup>.
> - Finally, balance the charge: the left side has a total charge of +7 before adding electrons, and the right side has +2, so 5e<sup>–</sup> are needed.
> 
> Remember OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

**Extract:**

i) Complete the half-equation for the reduction of manganate(VII) ions, MnO4–, to manganese(II) ions, Mn2+.

MnO4– (aq) + ........H+ (aq) + ........e– → Mn2+ (aq) + ........H2O (l)

The completed half-equation is:

i) Construct the half-equation for the oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+. Include state symbols.

The half-equation for the oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ is:
Fe2+ (aq) → Fe3+ (aq) + e–

Using your answers to parts (a) and (b), construct the overall ionic equation for the reaction between Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions and MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> ions.
parts.solution_md:
The overall ionic equation is:

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 5Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 5Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants and products
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing throughout

> **[exam-tip]**
> To combine the two half-equations, first balance the electrons. The MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> equation uses 5e<sup>–</sup> and the Fe<sup>2+</sup> equation produces 1e<sup>–</sup>, so multiply the Fe<sup>2+</sup> equation by 5. Then add the two equations and cancel the electrons:
>

parts.problem_md: Construct an equation for the reaction between ethanedioic acid, H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, and sodium hydroxide, NaOH.

> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethanedioic acid (H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) may also be written as (COOH)<sub>2</sub>. It is a diprotic acid, so it reacts with 2 moles of NaOH to form the salt sodium ethanedioate / sodium oxalate (Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) and water.

parts.problem_md:

15.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (aq) requires 10.30 cm<sup>3</sup> of a 0.25 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of NaOH for complete neutralisation, using phenolphthalein as the indicator.

moles of NaOH = $\frac{0.25\times10.30}{1000}$

- Calculate the moles of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (mole ratio H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> : NaOH = 1:2, from the equation in the previous part):

moles of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{2.575\times10^{-3}}{2}$

moles of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = 1.2875 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the concentration of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>:

concentration = $\frac{1.2875\times10^{-3}}{15.00} \times 1000$

concentration of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = **0.0858 mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of NaOH = 2.575 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for moles of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = 1.2875 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol (using 1:2 mole ratio)
> 
> 1 mark for concentration = 0.0858 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use the equation from the previous part (H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O) to find the mole ratio: 1 mole of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> reacts with 2 moles of NaOH.
> 
> The volume of KMnO<sub>4</sub> solution (12.35 cm<sup>3</sup>) given in the problem context is used to calculate the KMnO<sub>4</sub> concentration in a separate part. This calculation only requires the NaOH titration data.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

15.00 cm^3^ of the same H~2~C~2~O~4~ (aq) required 12.35 cm^3^ of potassium manganate(VII), KMnO~4~, solution for complete oxidation to carbon dioxide and water, in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid.

Construct the full redox equation, including state symbols, for this redox titration.
parts.solution_md:
To construct the full redox equation for the KMnO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> titration:

- Construct the two half-equations:

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 5e<sup>–</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**

H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (aq) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Combine the half-equations (multiply reduction x 2, oxidation x 5; cancel H<sup>+</sup> and e<sup>–</sup>):

2MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 6H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 5H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (aq) → 2Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 8H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 10CO<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> If state symbols are absent or incorrect, a maximum of 1 mark is deducted overall

> **[exam-tip]**
> The colour change at the end-point of a KMnO<sub>4</sub> redox titration is from purple (MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>) to very pale pink / colourless (Mn<sup>2+</sup>).
> 
> To derive the half-equations:
> 
> - MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> is reduced from +7 to +2 (gains 5 electrons per Mn)
> - H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> (loses 2 electrons per molecule)
> - Add H<sup>+</sup> and H<sub>2</sub>O to balance charge and atoms.
> 
> To combine:
> 
> - Multiply the reduction half-equation by 2 and the oxidation half-equation by 5 so that both sides have 10 electrons.
> - Then cancel the 10e<sup>–</sup> and 10H<sup>+</sup> that appear on both sides.

concentration of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = **0.0417 mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
This question is about transition metal complexes.

Define the terms ligand and complex ion.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definitions of the terms are:
> 
> - Ligand: a molecule or ion that has one or more lone pairs of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Complex ion: a molecule or ion formed by a central metal atom or ion surrounded by one or more ligands **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You should know the definitions of these key terms as they are commonly tested at the start of transition metal questions.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Ligand: a molecule or ion that has one or more lone pairs of electrons

Transition metals can form complexes with different ligands.

Identify **one** species from the following list that does not act as a ligand. Explain your answer.

CO          H<sub>2</sub>O          SCN<sup>–</sup>          H<sub>2</sub>
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The species that does not act as a ligand is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub> / hydrogen **[1 mark]**
> - H<sub>2</sub> has no lone pairs of electrons, so it cannot form a coordinate bond with the metal ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ligands must have at least one lone pair of electrons to donate to the central metal ion. Water (H<sub>2</sub>O), thiocyanate (SCN<sup>–</sup>) and carbon monoxide (CO) all have lone pairs and can act as ligands. Hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>) has no lone pairs, so it cannot.

parts.problem_md:
A complex ion contains one Co<sup>2+</sup> ion, four ammonia molecules and two chloride ions.

i) State the formula of this complex ion.

[1]

ii) State the geometry of this complex ion.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The formula of this complex ion is:
> 
> - [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>] **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The geometry of this complex ion is:
> 
> - Octahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each Cl<sup>–</sup> ligand has a charge of –1 and each NH<sub>3</sub> ligand is neutral. The Co<sup>2+</sup> ion has a charge of +2, so the overall charge on the complex is: +2 + (2 × –1) = 0. A neutral complex does not need square brackets with a charge.
> 
> With 6 ligands bonded to the central metal ion, the geometry is octahedral.

parts.problem_md:
The H<sub>2</sub>O ligands in [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> can be exchanged for other ligands.

Deduce the geometry of the complex ions formed after the following substitutions.

i) All the H<sub>2</sub>O ligands are exchanged for OH<sup>–</sup> ligands.

[1]

ii) The six H<sub>2</sub>O ligands are exchanged for four Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Exchanging all H<sub>2</sub>O ligands for OH<sup>–</sup> ligands:
> 
> - Octahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Exchanging six H<sub>2</sub>O ligands for four Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands:
> 
> - Tetrahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Shape' is accepted in place of 'geometry'.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When all six H<sub>2</sub>O ligands are replaced by six OH<sup>–</sup> ligands, the coordination number stays at 6, so the geometry remains octahedral.
> 
> When six H<sub>2</sub>O ligands are replaced by four Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands, the coordination number changes from 6 to 4. Four large ligands such as Cl<sup>–</sup> adopt a tetrahedral arrangement to minimise repulsion.

parts.problem_md:
Cisplatin can be used to treat some types of cancer.

It is a square planar transition metal complex with a central platinum(II) ion, two chloride ligands and two ammonia ligands.

Complete the three-dimensional diagram in Fig. 1.1 to show the shape of cisplatin. Label and state the value of one bond angle.

| Pt |
|---|

**Fig. 1.1**
parts.solution_md:
The completed three-dimensional structure and bond angle of cisplatin are:

![Structural diagram of cisplatin showing a central platinum atom bonded to two ammonia and two chloride ligands in a square planar arrangement](assets/010-structural-diagram-of-cisplatin-showing-a-centra.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct square planar structure with no overall charge shown
> 
> 1 mark for any bond angle correctly identified and labelled as 90°

> **[exam-tip]**
> Cisplatin is a cis-isomer, meaning the two NH<sub>3</sub> ligands are on the same side and the two Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands are on the same side. The Pt<sup>2+</sup> ion has a charge of +2; there are two Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands (each –1) and two neutral NH<sub>3</sub> ligands, giving an overall charge of zero — so no charge is shown outside the brackets.

parts.problem_md:
Iron(II) gluconate, C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>FeO<sub>14</sub>, is the active ingredient in some brands of iron supplements.

A student carries out an experiment to determine the mass of iron(II) gluconate in one tablet of an iron supplement, using the method below.

1. The student crushes two tablets and dissolves the powdered tablets in dilute sulfuric acid
2. The student makes up the solution from step 1 to 250.0 cm<sup>3</sup> in a volumetric flask.
3. The student then titrated 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> portions of the solution obtained in step 2 with 0.00200 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> potassium manganate(VII).

The student obtains a mean titre of 13.50 cm<sup>3</sup>.

In this titration, 1 mole of manganate(VII) ions reacts with 5 moles of iron(II) ions.

Calculate the mass, in mg, of iron(II) gluconate in **one** tablet. Show your working and give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the mass of iron(II) gluconate in one tablet:

- List the known values:

  - volume of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = 13.50 cm<sup>3</sup>
  - concentration of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = 0.00200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>
  - mole ratio MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> : Fe<sup>2+</sup> = 1:5
- Calculate the moles of MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>:

moles = $\frac{13.50}{1000}$ x 0.00200

moles of MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> = 2.70 x 10<sup>–5</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the aliquot:

moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> = 2.70 x 10<sup>–5</sup> x 5

moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>–4</sup> mol

- Scale to the full solution:

moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>–4</sup> x 10

moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>–3</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>FeO<sub>14</sub> and the mass in both tablets:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (12 x 12.0) + (22 x 1.0) + 55.8 + (14 x 16.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 445.8

mass in 2 tablets = 1.35 x 10<sup>–3</sup> x 445.8

mass in 2 tablets = 0.60183 g

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by 2 for one tablet and convert to mg:

mass in 1 tablet = $\frac{0.60183}{2}$ x 1000

mass in 1 tablet = **301 mg**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> = 2.70 x 10<sup>–5</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>–4</sup> mol **AND** in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>–3</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> = 445.8 **AND** mass in 2 tablets = 0.60183 g
> 
> 1 mark for final answer = 301 mg
> 
> Allow error carried forward if any error is correctly carried forward through subsequent steps

> **[exam-tip]**
> Take care with the *M*<sub>r</sub> calculation:
> 
> (12 x 12.0) + (22 x 1.0) + 55.8 + (14 x 16.0) = 445.8.
> 
> A common error is calculating the mass of Fe only rather than the mass of C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>FeO<sub>14</sub>, which gives 37.7 mg.
> 
> Remember the student crushed two tablets in step 1, so divide the total mass by 2 to get the mass per tablet. Convert from g to mg (x 1000) before rounding to 3 significant figures.

**Extract:**

A student carries out an experiment to determine the mass of iron(II) gluconate in one tablet of an iron supplement, using the method below.

1. The student crushes two tablets and dissolves the powdered tablets in dilute sulfuric acid
2. The student makes up the solution from step 1 to 250.0 cm^3^ in a volumetric flask.
3. The student then titrated 25.0 cm^3^ portions of the solution obtained in step 2 with 0.00200 mol dm^−3^ potassium manganate(VII).

The student obtains a mean titre of 13.50 cm^3^.

The typical concentration of a potassium manganate(VII) solution used in redox titrations is 0.0200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.

Use the information in part (a) to explain, quantitatively, why the student replaced this with a 0.00200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> potassium manganate(VII) solution for this titration.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The student used 0.00200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> instead of 0.0200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> because:
> 
> - A 0.0200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> potassium manganate(VII) solution would produce a titre of 1.35 cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - This would be hard to measure accurately from a burette
> **OR**
> This would have a high (percentage) error / uncertainty **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question asks you to use the **information** in part (a) (the data given in the experiment), not your calculated answer. The 0.00200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> solution gives a 13.50 cm<sup>3</sup> titre. Since 0.0200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> is ten times more concentrated, it would require only 13.50 ÷ 10 = 1.35 cm<sup>3</sup>.
> 
> A titre of 1.35 cm<sup>3</sup> is too small to measure accurately with a standard 50 cm<sup>3</sup> burette as it would have a very high percentage error.

parts.problem_md:
Some iron supplements contain iron(II) sulfate or iron(II) fumarate.

**Table 4.1** shows the information taken from the labels of two iron supplements, **A** and **B**.

**Table 4.1**

| **Iron supplement** | **Iron compound** | **Mass of iron compound in one tablet / mg** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Iron(II) sulfate, FeSO<sub>4</sub> | 180 |
| **B** | Iron(II) fumarate, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>FeO<sub>4</sub> | 210 |

State which iron supplement, **A** or **B**, would provide the greater mass of iron per tablet. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To determine which supplement provides the greater mass of iron per tablet:

- Calculate the mass of Fe in supplement **A**:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of FeSO<sub>4</sub> = 55.8 + 32.1 + (4 x 16.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of FeSO<sub>4</sub> = 151.9

mass of Fe in **A** = $\frac{55.8}{151.9}$ x 180

mass of Fe in **A** = 66.1 mg

- Calculate the mass of Fe in supplement **B**:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>FeO<sub>4</sub> = (4 x 12.0) + (2 x 1.0) + 55.8 + (4 x 16.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>FeO<sub>4</sub> = 169.8

mass of Fe in **B** = $\frac{55.8}{169.8}$ x 210

mass of Fe in **B** = 69.0 mg

**[1 mark]**

Supplement **B** provides the greater mass of iron per tablet (69.0 mg > 66.1 mg) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for mass of Fe in **A** = 66 mg **AND** mass of Fe in **B** = 69 mg (both correct)
> 
> Accept values to 3 sf: A = 66.1 mg, B = 69.0 mg
> 
> 1 mark for supplement **B** identified as providing the greater mass of iron per tablet

> **[exam-tip]**
> Iron fumarate contains iron as Fe<sup>2+</sup>: the fumarate ion (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup>) pairs with Fe<sup>2+</sup>, giving iron(II) fumarate.
> 
> Calculate the mass of iron (not the mass of the compound) in each tablet. The *M*<sub>r</sub> values needed are FeSO<sub>4</sub> = 151.9 and C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>FeO<sub>4</sub> = 169.8.

parts.problem_md:
Complex ions have a central transition metal ion surrounded by ligands.

Explain why the ammonium ion cannot act as a ligand.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ammonium ion cannot act as a ligand because:
> 
> - Ammonium ions do not have a lone pair (of electrons for bonding) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A ligand must have a lone pair of electrons to form a dative covalent (coordinate) bond with the transition metal ion. In this type of bond, both electrons are donated by the ligand.

parts.problem_md: Explain why the complex ions [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> both form coloured solutions but exhibit different colours to each other.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> form coloured solutions with different colours because:
> 
> - The d orbitals / sub-shells split (into two different energy levels)
> **OR**
> The d orbitals / sub-shells change from degenerate to non-degenerate **[1 mark]**
> - Different ligands lead to different energy level splits **[1 mark]**
> - The difference in energy / Δ*E* leads to different frequencies / wavelengths / photons of light being absorbed
> **OR**
> The difference in energy / Δ*E* is absorbed by an electron (being promoted) **[1 mark]**
> - The different unabsorbed frequencies / wavelengths / photons are reflected / transmitted **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Factors affecting the colour of a complex ion include the type and size of ligands, the identity and nuclear charge of the metal ion, its oxidation state, and the shape of the complex. In this case, both complexes have the same metal ion, oxidation state, and shape. The ligand is the only structural difference.
> 
> When a ligand coordinates to the cobalt ion, it causes the 3d energy level to split into two sub-levels. Different ligands cause different degrees of splitting, so different frequencies of light are absorbed. The colour observed is the complementary colour to the light that is absorbed.

parts.problem_md:
Hydrated chromium(III) chloride, CrCl<sub>3</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O, dissolves in water to form a number of different complex ions containing both chloride and water ligands.

The general formula of these complex ions is [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>x</sub>(Cl)<sub>y</sub>]<sup>(3–y)+</sup>

In an experiment, 0.10 mol of a complex reacted with excess silver nitrate solution to produce 0.20 mol of silver chloride.

Chloride ions which are ligands within the complex do not react with silver nitrate.

Deduce the formula of this chromium(III) complex ion. Explain your reasoning.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Deducing the formula of the chromium(III) complex ion:
> 
> - The formula is [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>(Cl)]<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - 0.10 mol of complex produces 0.20 mol AgCl, so 0.20 mol of chloride ions are free in solution
> **OR**
> 0.10 mol of chloride ions remain coordinated as ligands
> **OR**
> One chloride ion acts as a ligand **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The ionic equation for the reaction of chloride ions with silver nitrate is Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq) → AgCl (s), showing a 1:1 molar ratio.
> 
> Since 0.10 mol of complex produces 0.20 mol of AgCl, 0.20 mol of chloride ions are free in solution. Each formula unit releases 2 free Cl<sup>–</sup> ions. From CrCl<sub>3</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O, there are 3 Cl<sup>–</sup> in total, so 1 must remain as a ligand within the complex.
> 
> With one Cl<sup>–</sup> ligand and using the general formula [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>x</sub>(Cl)]<sup>2+</sup>, the complex is octahedral with six coordinate bonds, giving x = 5.
